questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has 10 months of tripping over her right foot and, more recently, weakness of her left hand. There is wasting of the left first dorsal interosseous with fasciculations, brisk reflexes in all limbs and an upgoing right plantar. Sensation and eye movements are normal. She has no pain.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Progressive asymmetric weakness over months with mixed UMN and LMN signs and normal sensation and eye movements is MND.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: wasting of the left first dorsal interosseous with fasciculations
Sensation and eye movements are normal
steps.x: Mixed UMN and LMN signs, progressive, with sensation spared.

elim: Usually causes neck pain and sensory signs, and cannot explain foot drop with leg LMN signs alone.
Acute, ascending, with areflexia, not progressive mixed signs over 10 months.
Causes UMN and sensory signs but not wasting and fasciculations.
Fatigable weakness with normal reflexes and no wasting or fasciculations.

steps.x: UMN + LMN signs + normal sensation and eye movements = MND.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has 6 months of progressive weakness and stiffness of both hands. There is wasting of the thenar eminences with fasciculations and brisk biceps and triceps reflexes. Sensation is normal. The doctor flicks the distal phalanx of his middle finger.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on this test?
o: Absent response with sensory loss in the fingers
Fatigue of the finger flexors on repetition
Flexion of the thumb and index finger (positive Hoffman's sign)
questions.e: Hoffman's sign, an UMN sign elicited by flicking the distal phalanx of the middle finger, may be positive in MND.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on this test?

clues: flicks the distal phalanx of his middle finger
steps.x: UMN signs in the arms; the test described is Hoffman's.

elim: Sensation is normal in MND.
Not the response tested by Hoffman's sign.
Fatigability suggests myasthenia gravis.
Suggests a radiculopathy.

steps.x: Hoffman's sign = UMN sign; may be positive in MND.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man is referred with 8 months of progressive weakness of his right arm with wasting and fasciculations. His reflexes are brisk. The neurologist is considering motor neurone disease and examines him carefully for features that would point to another diagnosis.
questions.q: Which finding would make motor neurone disease least likely?
o: Brisk reflexes in a wasted arm
Loss of pin-prick sensation in a glove distribution
questions.e: Sensory examination is characteristically normal in MND, so sensory loss points to another cause such as a neuropathy or myelopathy.

steps.x: The question asks: Which finding would make motor neurone disease least likely?

clues: progressive weakness of his right arm
steps.x: Mixed UMN/LMN signs; the question asks which finding argues against MND.

elim: Mixed UMN and LMN signs are typical of MND.
Widespread fasciculations support MND.
Eye movements are characteristically spared in MND.
An UMN sign that fits MND.

steps.x: MND spares sensation and eye movements. Sensory signs suggest another diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has 5 months of slurred speech and difficulty swallowing liquids. Her voice has become quiet and she has lost 5 kg. Her limbs show brisk reflexes and some wasting of the hands. Sensation and eye movements are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her tongue?
questions.e: Bulbar ALS causes dysarthria, dysphagia, weight loss, hypophonic speech and tongue fasciculations, with a reduced jaw jerk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her tongue?

clues: slurred speech and difficulty swallowing liquids
Sensation and eye movements are normal
steps.x: Bulbar symptoms plus limb UMN and LMN signs.

elim: A smooth red tongue from B12 or iron deficiency.
A benign pattern of the tongue surface, not neurological.
Seen in hypothyroidism, acromegaly or amyloid.
Would be sudden with other stroke signs.

steps.x: Bulbar ALS: dysarthria, dysphagia, weight loss, tongue fasciculations.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man has newly diagnosed motor neurone disease. His symptoms began with slurred speech and choking, and examination shows tongue wasting and fasciculations with no limb involvement yet. He asks his neurologist which form of MND carries the worst outlook.
questions.q: Which form of motor neurone disease has the worst prognosis?
o: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis with limb onset
questions.e: Progressive bulbar palsy affects the lower cranial nerves (IX, X, XII) and has the worst prognosis, with median survival around 2 to 3 years.

steps.x: The question asks: Which form of motor neurone disease has the worst prognosis?
Bulbar-only disease of the lower cranial nerves.

elim: The most common form, with a better outlook than bulbar palsy.
UMN only, generally slower.
LMN only, generally a better prognosis than bulbar palsy.
Limb onset carries a better prognosis than bulbar onset.

steps.x: Progressive bulbar palsy: IX, X, XII, worst prognosis (~2 to 3 years).

questions.stem: A 54 year old woman has 3 years of slowly worsening stiffness of both legs and a spastic gait. Reflexes are brisk throughout with upgoing plantars and clonus. There is no wasting and no fasciculations, and EMG shows no denervation. Sensation is normal and MRI brain and spine is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Primary lateral sclerosis is the MND variant with UMN signs only.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: MRI brain and spine is normal
steps.x: Pure UMN signs with compression excluded.

elim: ALS has both UMN and LMN signs; she has no LMN signs.
Her MRI spine is normal.
She has no bulbar features.
This is LMN only; she has only UMN signs.

steps.x: UMN only = primary lateral sclerosis. LMN only = progressive muscular atrophy.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has 9 months of progressive weakness of both arms. There is wasting of the shoulder girdle and hands with widespread fasciculations. Reflexes in the arms are absent and plantars are downgoing. Sensation is normal. EMG shows widespread denervation with normal sensory conduction.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Progressive muscular atrophy is the MND variant with LMN signs only: weakness, wasting and fasciculations without UMN signs.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: wasting of the shoulder girdle and hands with widespread fasciculations
Reflexes in the arms are absent and plantars are downgoing
steps.x: LMN signs only, with sensation spared.

elim: ALS has mixed UMN and LMN signs; he has none of the UMN signs.
Causes sensory involvement and slowed conduction.
No wasting or fasciculations, and fatigable weakness.
This is UMN only.

steps.x: LMN only = progressive muscular atrophy.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has had amyotrophic lateral sclerosis for 3 years. He is wheelchair-bound and fed through a PEG tube. His family ask what is most likely to cause his death so they can plan his care. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most common cause of death in motor neurone disease?
questions.e: Respiratory failure from respiratory muscle weakness is the most common cause of death in MND.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most common cause of death in motor neurone disease?

clues: what is most likely to cause his death
steps.x: Advanced ALS.

elim: The heart muscle is not affected in MND.
Not a feature of MND.
Can occur with immobility but is not the most common cause.
Not a feature of MND.

steps.x: MND death is usually from respiratory failure.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman has just been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis after EMG. Her cognition is currently normal. Her husband asks whether any change in her personality or thinking may develop as the disease progresses. She has weakness of her right hand and left leg. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which condition is most strongly associated with motor neurone disease?
questions.e: Frontotemporal dementia is an important association of MND, linked through C9orf72 and TDP-43 pathology.

steps.x: The question asks: Which condition is most strongly associated with motor neurone disease?

clues: change in her personality or thinking
steps.x: Personality change in ALS.

elim: Not the dementia linked with MND.
Associated with parkinsonism and visual hallucinations, not MND.
Causes gait apraxia, incontinence and dementia; not linked to MND.
Linked to vascular risk factors, not MND.

steps.x: MND is associated with frontotemporal dementia.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has 6 months of progressive weakness of his left leg with wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes. Sensation is normal. His father died of MND aged 45 and his aunt developed frontotemporal dementia in her 50s.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Familial ALS has a prominent family history and early onset; C9orf72 (also linked to FTD) and SOD1 are implicated.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: His father died of MND aged 45
steps.x: Very early onset with MND and FTD in the family.

elim: Causes pure UMN signs in both legs, not wasting and fasciculations.
Causes chorea and cognitive decline, not mixed UMN and LMN weakness.
Does not cause wasting and fasciculations.
Presents in infancy.

steps.x: Young onset + family history of MND/FTD = familial ALS (C9orf72, SOD1).

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman is diagnosed with motor neurone disease after 1 year of progressive weakness. She has wasting and fasciculations of her right hand with brisk reflexes and an upgoing plantar on the right. She has no bulbar symptoms. She asks which type of MND she has.
questions.q: Which is the most likely type of motor neurone disease?
questions.e: ALS is the most common type of MND, and spinal ALS, with mixed UMN and LMN limb signs, is the most common variant.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely type of motor neurone disease?

clues: wasting and fasciculations of her right hand with brisk reflexes
steps.x: Mixed UMN and LMN limb signs.

elim: UMN signs only.
She has no bulbar symptoms.
LMN signs only.
A childhood genetic disorder, not adult MND with UMN signs.

steps.x: Mixed UMN + LMN limb signs = ALS, the most common MND.

questions.stem: A 67 year old man has 7 months of weakness of both hands with wasting and fasciculations, brisk reflexes in the legs and upgoing plantars. He also has fasciculations of the tongue. He has no neck pain, sensation is normal throughout and bladder function is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Normal sensation and tongue fasciculations (above the neck) distinguish MND from cervical myelopathy as a cause of mixed UMN and LMN signs.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Mixed signs, sensation spared, and LMN signs above the neck.

elim: Would not cause tongue fasciculations and usually causes sensory signs.
Would not cause wasting and fasciculations.
Causes fatigable weakness without fasciculations or brisk reflexes.
Causes dissociated sensory loss in a cape distribution.

steps.x: Tongue fasciculations + normal sensation: MND, not cervical myelopathy.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has 6 months of weakness of his left arm. He has noticed twitching of the arm muscles at night. On examination the left biceps is visibly wasted with fasciculations. Sensation is normal. Eye movements are normal. His temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which other finding is most likely in the wasted arm?
o: Ptosis worse at the end of the day
questions.e: MND characteristically produces UMN signs, such as brisk reflexes, in the same limb as LMN signs such as wasting and fasciculations.

steps.x: The question asks: Which other finding is most likely in the wasted arm?
LMN signs with sensation spared: look for coexisting UMN signs.

elim: A parkinsonian sign.
Sensation is spared in MND.
A cerebellar sign.
Fatigable ptosis suggests myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: MND = UMN and LMN signs together, often in the same limb.

questions.stem: A 72 year old woman with bulbar-onset ALS has lost 8 kg over 4 months. Her appetite is good but meals take an hour, she coughs during drinks and food sticks in her throat. Her speech is slurred. Her TFTs and HbA1c are normal and there is no evidence of cancer.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her weight loss?
questions.e: Bulbar ALS causes dysarthria, dysphagia and weight loss; she cannot eat enough despite a good appetite.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely cause of her weight loss?
Swallowing difficulty in bulbar disease.

elim: Her appetite is good.
Her TFTs are normal.
There are no bowel symptoms; the problem is swallowing.
There is no evidence of cancer and the swallowing problem explains it.

steps.x: Bulbar ALS: dysphagia leads to weight loss and aspiration risk.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman has 7 months of progressive weakness of her right leg and left hand, with wasting, fasciculations and brisk reflexes. Sensation and eye movements are normal. Her CK is mildly raised. The neurologist suspects motor neurone disease.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: EMG with nerve conduction studies is the gold standard and first-line investigation for MND, showing widespread denervation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
Suspected MND on clinical grounds.

elim: Test for myasthenia gravis.
Not diagnostic for MND.
Used to exclude other causes, not to diagnose MND.
For myopathy; a mildly raised CK is common in denervation.

steps.x: Diagnose MND with EMG/NCS. MRI only excludes mimics.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man with suspected motor neurone disease has 5 months of hand weakness with wasting and fasciculations and brisk reflexes. He has no numbness. He has electromyography and nerve conduction studies. Eye movements are normal. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
questions.q: Which result is most likely on his sensory nerve conduction studies?
o: Absent sensory potentials in all limbs
Reduced sensory potentials in a median nerve distribution only
questions.e: EMG shows denervation in MND but sensory nerve conduction is normal because sensory pathways are spared.

steps.x: The question asks: Which result is most likely on his sensory nerve conduction studies?
MND spares sensory neurons.

elim: Suggests a sensory neuronopathy or neuropathy.
Suggests a demyelinating neuropathy.
Suggests demyelinating neuropathy.
Suggests carpal tunnel syndrome.

steps.x: MND: EMG shows denervation; sensory conduction is normal.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has 6 months of weakness of both arms with wasting and brisk leg reflexes. EMG shows denervation in her arms. Before confirming motor neurone disease, her neurologist requests an MRI of the cervical spine. She has no neck pain and sensation is normal.
questions.q: Which is the main purpose of this MRI?
o: To exclude a structural or compressive cause
To grade the severity of motor neurone disease
To look for demyelinating plaques that confirm MND
questions.e: MRI brain or spine is used to exclude structural or compressive causes such as cervical myelopathy, not to diagnose MND.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the main purpose of this MRI?

clues: weakness of both arms with wasting and brisk leg reflexes
steps.x: Arm LMN plus leg UMN signs could also come from cord compression in the neck.

elim: MRI does not diagnose MND.
MRI is not used for this.
Plaques suggest MS, and they do not confirm MND.
Unrelated to spinal imaging.

steps.x: MRI excludes mimics such as cervical myelopathy. EMG diagnoses MND.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man has 4 months of slurred speech and difficulty swallowing with tongue fasciculations. Limb examination shows brisk reflexes. Sensation and eye movements are normal. EMG shows denervation in the tongue and limbs. A brainstem lesion has not yet been excluded.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: With bulbar features, MRI brain excludes structural brainstem causes; it does not diagnose MND itself.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate investigation?

clues: A brainstem lesion has not yet been excluded
steps.x: Bulbar symptoms need a structural brainstem cause excluded.

elim: Assesses swallowing but does not exclude a brainstem lesion.
Not the next step in a bulbar presentation.
Does not exclude structural brainstem disease.
Not used to diagnose MND.

steps.x: MRI brain/spine excludes structural causes before MND is confirmed.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman with newly diagnosed ALS is about to start riluzole. She asks what benefit she can expect from it. She is walking with a stick and swallowing normally. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most accurate statement about riluzole?
o: It improves muscle strength within weeks
It is only used once respiratory failure develops
It slows progression and extends survival by a small amount
questions.e: Riluzole is the first-line disease-modifying treatment; it slows progression and extends survival by only a small amount (historically about 3 months).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most accurate statement about riluzole?
Counselling about the only disease-modifying drug.

elim: There is no cure.
It slows decline; it does not restore strength.
It is started early as disease-modifying treatment.
It does not reverse signs.

steps.x: Riluzole: slows progression; survival gain is small (~3 months).

questions.stem: A 65 year old man has just been diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis after EMG. He has weakness of his left hand and right leg but walks unaided and swallows normally. He asks for a medicine that can slow the disease. He has normal liver function.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate disease-modifying treatment?
questions.e: Riluzole, an antiglutamatergic drug, is the first-line disease-modifying treatment for MND.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate disease-modifying treatment?

clues: medicine that can slow the disease
steps.x: He wants a disease-modifying drug.

elim: Used in GBS or CIDP, not MND.
Used in GBS and myasthenic crisis, not MND.
Steroids do not slow MND.
Symptomatic treatment for myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: MND disease-modifying drug = riluzole.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman with MND has had two chest infections from aspiration in 3 months. She has lost 12% of her body weight. Speech and language therapy confirm unsafe swallow despite thickened fluids. Her respiratory function is still adequate.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term nutritional support?
questions.e: A PEG tube provides long-term nutritional support in MND when swallowing is unsafe or weight is falling.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate long-term nutritional support?
Unsafe swallow and major weight loss in a progressive disease.

elim: Her swallow is unsafe, so oral intake risks aspiration.
For short-term feeding, not long-term.
Already tried and unsafe.
Not needed when the gut works.

steps.x: Long-term feeding in MND = PEG.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with ALS has weakness of ankle dorsiflexion on the right and has tripped twice this month. He also has stiffness in his legs. He swallows and speaks normally and his weight is stable. He is taking riluzole.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Supportive care in MND includes physiotherapy (mobility, splints, spasticity), speech and language therapy and nutritional support.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Mobility problem with normal bulbar and respiratory function.

elim: Used for movement disorders, not MND.
For respiratory failure, which he does not have.
He swallows normally with stable weight.
Riluzole should continue.

steps.x: MND long-term care is multidisciplinary: physio, SLT and nutrition.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man with ALS has 2 months of morning headaches, poor sleep and daytime sleepiness. He becomes breathless lying flat. His respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Advanced MND with respiratory failure (morning headaches, orthopnoea, hypercapnia) is treated with non-invasive ventilation.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Symptoms and gas of nocturnal hypoventilation from respiratory muscle weakness.

elim: For obstructive sleep apnoea; it does not support weak respiratory muscles.
Can worsen hypercapnia without supporting ventilation.
Not effective in MND.
Steroids do not help MND respiratory failure.

steps.x: MND respiratory failure → NIV.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman with ALS has had 2 months of slurred speech. Her family find her hard to understand on the phone. She swallows normally and her weight is stable. She is taking riluzole. Her oxygen saturation is 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Supportive care in MND includes speech and language therapy for dysarthria and communication aids.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
Dysarthria without swallowing or breathing problems.

elim: No respiratory failure.
She swallows normally with stable weight.
Riluzole should continue.
Not indicated.

steps.x: Dysarthria in MND → SLT.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man with ALS has wasting and fasciculations of his hands together with brisk reflexes and upgoing plantars. A medical student asks which neurons are affected to produce this mixture of signs. Sensation and eye movements are normal. His pulse rate is 74 bpm.
questions.q: Which structures degenerate in this condition?
o: Corticospinal tract neurons and anterior horn cells
questions.e: MND is progressive degeneration of upper motor neurons (corticospinal tracts) and lower motor neurons (anterior horn cells and cranial nerve nuclei).

steps.x: The question asks: Which structures degenerate in this condition?
LMN and UMN signs together.

elim: This would cause a movement disorder such as Parkinson's.
Cause ataxia, not weakness with fasciculations.
Sensory neurons, which are spared in MND.
Affected in myasthenia gravis.

steps.x: MND = loss of both UMNs (corticospinal) and LMNs (anterior horn, cranial nuclei).

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman with ALS has stiff legs with brisk knee jerks, ankle clonus and upgoing plantars. Her husband asks why her reflexes are so brisk when her muscles are weak. There is also wasting of her hands. Sensation is normal. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her brisk reflexes?
o: Excess acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
Loss of descending inhibitory control from upper motor neurons
questions.e: UMN loss causes spasticity, hyperreflexia and Babinski's sign through loss of descending inhibitory control.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of her brisk reflexes?

clues: brisk knee jerks, ankle clonus and upgoing plantars
steps.x: These are UMN signs.

elim: Causes wasting and fasciculations (LMN), not brisk reflexes.
Not the mechanism.
Not the mechanism.
Sensation is spared in MND.

steps.x: UMN loss → loss of descending inhibition → spasticity, hyperreflexia, Babinski.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with ALS has wasting of his hand muscles and frequent visible twitching under the skin of his arms and thighs. He asks why his muscles twitch and shrink. His reflexes are brisk and sensation is normal. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his wasting and fasciculations?
o: Denervation of muscle fibres from lower motor neuron loss
Loss of descending inhibition from upper motor neurons
questions.e: LMN loss causes muscle wasting, weakness and fasciculations from denervation of muscle fibres.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his wasting and fasciculations?
These are LMN signs.

elim: Myasthenia gravis; no fasciculations or wasting.
He has no pain; this is denervation.
Causes spasticity and hyperreflexia.
Myositis causes proximal weakness with high CK, not fasciculations.

steps.x: LMN loss → denervation → wasting, weakness, fasciculations.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman develops progressive limb weakness with mixed UMN and LMN signs. Her mother and grandfather had MND. Genetic testing shows a mutation in the gene for an antioxidant enzyme that normally neutralises superoxide radicals. She has no cognitive change.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of motor neuron death from this mutation?
o: Toxic gain-of-function of mutant superoxide dismutase
questions.e: SOD1 mutations cause a toxic gain-of-function in superoxide dismutase that contributes to motor neuron death in a subset of familial ALS.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of motor neuron death from this mutation?

clues: Her mother and grandfather had MND
steps.x: Familial ALS; the enzyme described is superoxide dismutase (SOD1).

elim: MND is not autoimmune.
This describes C9orf72, not an enzyme gene.
Causes Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Causes Huntington's disease.

steps.x: SOD1 = toxic gain-of-function in familial ALS.

questions.stem: A 56 year old man has ALS and has developed disinhibition and loss of empathy. Genetic testing shows a C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansion. His daughter asks why the same gene causes both his weakness and his personality change. His mother had dementia in her 50s. His pulse rate is 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely shared pathology linking the two conditions?
questions.e: C9orf72 repeat expansion is the most common genetic cause of familial ALS and links MND to frontotemporal dementia through shared TDP-43 pathology.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely shared pathology linking the two conditions?
ALS with FTD features and C9orf72.

elim: Seen in Alzheimer's disease.
Seen in Parkinson's and Lewy body dementia.
Typical of Alzheimer's and some FTD subtypes, but not the link here.
Seen in Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

steps.x: C9orf72 links MND and FTD via TDP-43.

questions.stem: A 64 year old woman with ALS is prescribed the only licensed disease-modifying drug in the UK. She is a retired chemist and asks which excess neurotransmitter the drug is designed to counter. She walks with a frame and swallows normally. Her liver function tests are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?
o: Increases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction
questions.e: Riluzole is antiglutamatergic and is thought to reduce glutamate-mediated excitotoxicity.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of action of this drug?
The drug is riluzole.

elim: Not the mechanism of riluzole.
This is pyridostigmine, used in myasthenia gravis.
Not the mechanism of riluzole.
MND is not autoimmune.

steps.x: Riluzole = antiglutamatergic; reduces excitotoxicity.
